opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most interesting aspects of the DeepSeek paper. With R1-Zero, they showed that you can take a base model and go straight to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, things like math answers you can check or code that has to pass tests, and the model learns to reason on its own. You see these emergent behaviors: the chains of thought get longer over training, and the model starts doing things like backtracking or checking its own work, the famous "aha moment," without anyone showing it examples of that.

That's scientifically really exciting, because it suggests the reasoning ability is somewhat latent in the base model and RL just draws it out. But R1-Zero had practical problems. The outputs were often hard to read. It would mix languages, switching between English and Chinese mid-thought, and the formatting was messy. For a research artifact that's fine, but for a model people actually use it isn't.

So with R1 they added a cold-start phase: a small amount of supervised fine-tuning on curated long chain-of-thought examples before RL. That does a few things. It gives the model a readable format and a consistent language to begin with. It also seems to stabilize and speed up the early part of RL, since you're not waiting for the model to stumble onto good reasoning behavior from scratch. Then they layered on more stages: rejection sampling to build a bigger SFT set, mixing in general non-reasoning data, and another round of RL for helpfulness and harmlessness.

The trade-off, as I see it, is purity and scalability versus control and efficiency. Going directly to RL is conceptually simpler. You aren't limited by the quality or style of human-written demonstrations, so in principle the model could find reasoning strategies better than what you'd teach it. Starting with SFT puts a prior on the model. That helps with usability and stability, but you're partly shaping its reasoning in your own image.

This connects to our work on s1. We found you don't need a huge SFT dataset to get strong reasoning. About a thousand carefully chosen, high-quality, difficult, diverse examples got you a long way, plus test-time techniques like budget forcing to control how long the model thinks. So the SFT side can be very cheap if you're careful about data selection, and much of the reasoning capability is already in a good base model. In practice, I think the right answer is often a bit of both: a small, high-quality SFT warm start to get the format and behavior roughly right, then RL to push performance beyond what the demonstrations alone can teach.

r001.rationale: The response says R1-Zero outputs had messy formatting and that R1’s SFT warm start provides a readable, consistent format.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that R1-Zero was really the more scientifically interesting experiment, and R1 was the more practically useful model. With R1-Zero, they took the base model and went straight to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, so just math and code problems where you can check the answer, and no human-written reasoning traces at all. And the exciting finding was that the long chain-of-thought behavior, the self-verification, the backtracking, the "wait, let me reconsider" moments, all of that emerged on its own just from the reward signal. Nobody taught the model to do that. That was the big result, because it suggests you don't need expensive human annotation of reasoning to get reasoning.

But the trade-off is that pure RL from a base model gives you a model that's kind of ugly to use. R1-Zero had issues with readability, it would mix languages mid-thought, switch between English and Chinese, the outputs weren't well formatted. The RL only cares about getting the right final answer, so it has no incentive to make the reasoning legible to a human. And there's also a stability and efficiency question. Starting RL from a base model means the early phase is noisy, because the model doesn't really know what a good response even looks like yet, so a lot of the exploration is wasted.

So what they did with R1 is essentially bootstrap from R1-Zero. They used a small amount of cold-start SFT data, a few thousand long chain-of-thought examples, some of which came from R1-Zero outputs that were cleaned up and made readable, and some from other sources. That gives the model a good prior over the format and the style before you start RL. Then you run the RL, and after that there's another round where you sample from the RL model, filter for correctness, mix in general-purpose data, do another SFT, and then a final RL stage for alignment and helpfulness.

The way I'd summarize it is that SFT is giving the model a prior, and RL is doing the search. If your prior is terrible, the search takes longer and goes to weird places. If your prior is good, RL converges faster and the final model is more usable. The cost is that you've now injected human preferences about what reasoning should look like, so you've constrained the space a bit. You might lose some of the more alien but effective strategies the model would otherwise discover. For most practical purposes that trade is clearly worth it, but from a research perspective, R1-Zero is the one that tells you something about what's actually possible, which is why I think it got so much attention relative to how much it was actually used.

And I'd add that this connects to what we found with s1, where even a very small amount of carefully selected SFT data, like a thousand examples, gets you a surprising amount of the way there. So the cold-start phase doesn't need to be large, it just needs to establish the right behavior, and then test-time compute or RL can do the rest.

r001.rationale: The response says R1-Zero’s RL-only outputs were poorly formatted and unreadable, and explains that cold-start SFT establishes the desired format and style.

astra-6.text:
I think the trade-off is between giving the model a useful starting point and seeing how much it can discover through reinforcement learning alone. With R1-Zero, you go directly from the base model into RL. You reward it for getting the answer right, and the interesting question is whether reasoning behaviors emerge without explicitly showing it examples of how to reason.

Starting with supervised fine-tuning, as in R1, gives the model examples of the kind of response you want. That can make the subsequent reinforcement learning easier and help with readability and consistency. But you’re also shaping its behavior through the examples you choose.

So R1-Zero is particularly interesting as a demonstration of what RL alone can produce. For building a useful assistant, the supervised starting point is a practical way to guide that process. You still let the model improve through RL, but it doesn’t have to discover everything from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised fine-tuning can improve readability and consistency, but does not state that skipping it risks outputs failing to follow the desired format.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the trade-off is really between giving the model a useful starting point and letting it discover the behavior itself. With R1-Zero, you take the base model and go straight into reinforcement learning. If you can verify whether an answer is correct, you can reward that outcome without having to demonstrate every step of the reasoning. And the interesting result is that a lot of reasoning behavior can emerge from that.

But getting the answer right doesn’t necessarily mean the response is readable or easy to use. You can get language mixing or reasoning that’s difficult to follow. The supervised fine-tuning stage in R1 gives the model a small amount of guidance about what a good reasoning response should look like before you start reinforcement learning.

So I’d view R1-Zero as a really interesting demonstration of what reinforcement learning can produce on its own, while R1 is a more practical recipe. You provide an initial direction through examples, and then use reinforcement learning to improve beyond that starting point.

r001.rationale: The response says R1-Zero outputs can mix languages or be difficult to follow, but it does not clearly state that skipping supervised fine-tuning risks outputs failing to follow the desired format.
